paras: The lynching of Nathan Bonnet took place at Williston, South Carolina, on the night of Wednesday, September 13, 1882, when a body of lynchers overpowered the jailer, took Bonnet, a Black prisoner, from the town jail, hanged him and riddled his body with bullets. Bonnet, described as seventeen years old, had been accused of entering a white man's house at midnight and attempting to rape his daughter, and was said to have confessed in jail. A short wire dispatch carried the story across the country within days, often under headlines approving the killing, while a South Carolina paper published a fuller account that praised it.

According to the Abbeville Press and Banner, Bonnett entered the room of a 15-year-old girl, the daughter of 'a highly respectable gentleman of Williston,' carrying a cloth soaked in chloroform and a pocket knife. The paper said he applied the cloth and began cutting off her garments until a younger sister came in and raised the alarm, and that he fled, leaving his knife behind. The knife was given to Trial Justice McMitchel, and the paper credited it with leading to Bonnett's detection; when approached he reportedly confessed and produced a gold ring taken from the girl's finger. The wire version was briefer, saying only that he had entered the house at midnight and attempted to rape the daughter, and that he 'had confessed his guilt.'

Bonnet was held in the Williston town jail until Wednesday night, when 'a body of lynchers' overpowered the jailer and took him out. The Abbeville paper put the party at about one hundred and fifty men and said they hanged him to a tree; the wire reported that he was 'immediately hanged and his body riddled with bullets.' Neither account says where the tree stood or whether anyone watched.
No report of an inquest, an arrest of any member of the mob, or other official action appears in the coverage.

The news first went out as a Williston dispatch of September 15, printed by the Rock Island Argus under the headline 'Quite Right' and by the Sacramento Daily Record-Union as 'Negro Lynched by a Mob.' A longer Charleston dispatch of the same date ran on September 16 in papers from Savannah to Lancaster, Pennsylvania, and St. Paul, where headlines included 'A Negro Fiend Lynched,' 'Summary Justice' and, in the Omaha Bee, 'The Proper Caper.' Weekly papers in Ohio, Michigan, Iowa, New Hampshire, Texas and Montana repeated the item through September 21, usually as a single line in a digest of the week's news, and the Stark County Democrat called Bonnet a 'colored rapist.'

Copying garbled the details: the victim appeared as Nathan Bonnett, Bonnel, Bonnell, Nathan Bennett and, in the Dallas Herald, John Bennett, and several papers moved the lynching to Charleston or to North Carolina. Two digests mentioned only that a negro had been hanged by a mob 'at Charleston' on the same day as legal executions in Chicago and Mound City, Illinois. The fullest South Carolina report, 'The Williston Lynching' in the Abbeville Press and Banner of September 27, endorsed the killing, saying it left the impression that 'the women of our county are going to be protected' and that Bonnett had 'merited such a fate.'

The fuller Charleston dispatch dated the seizure to Wednesday night, and one brief carried a dateline of the 13th, while shortened versions said the lynching happened 'to-day' or 'yesterday,' meaning September 15, apparently reading the wire's date as the date of the killing. The girl was described as 'a little white girl' in the short wire and as fifteen in the Abbeville account.

reader.title: Lynching of Nathan Bonnet
bases: A body of lynchers took a Black prisoner accused of attempted rape from the Williston town jail, overpowering the jailer, and hanged and shot him (A4, A7, A20).

Every account reports that a mob ('lynchers', about 150 men per A20) took Bonnet from jail by overpowering the jailer and hanged and shot him, without trial, as punishment for an alleged attempted rape of a white girl (A1, A7, A20).

The Charleston/Williston wire carried nationally (A1, A7, A8) and the separate, more detailed South Carolina account in the Abbeville Press and Banner (A20) agree on the jail seizure, hanging and shooting of a Black man named Bonnet or Bonnett at Williston.

accounts.label: Charleston wire report
accounts.gist: A negro, Nathan Bonnet, aged seventeen, entered a white citizen's Williston house at midnight and attempted to rape his daughter; on Wednesday night lynchers overpowered the jailer, took him from the town jail, hanged him and riddled his body with bullets; he had confessed.

accounts.label: Williston short wire
accounts.gist: Lynchers hanged Nathan Bonnet and riddled his body with bullets; he tried to rape a little white girl and confessed in jail; some versions date it 'to-day', Sept. 15, one datelines it the 13th.

accounts.label: Abbeville Press and Banner (South Carolina)
accounts.gist: Bonnett chloroformed a 15-year-old girl and cut her garments with a knife, fled when her younger sister raised the alarm, was traced through the dropped knife by Trial Justice McMitchel, confessed and produced her ring, and was taken by about 150 men, hanged to a tree and shot.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Quite Right', 'The Proper Caper' and 'Summary Justice' presented the lynching as deserved.
The Savannah Morning News headed the wire 'A Negro Fiend Lynched'; the Stark County Democrat called Bonnet a 'colored rapist'.
The Abbeville Press and Banner said the lynching showed 'the women of our county are going to be protected' and that Bonnett 'merited such a fate'.
Many northern and western papers ran the brief without comment under neutral headings like 'Lynched' or in news digests.

conflicts.note: All describe the same Williston jail lynching; the South Carolina account (A20) and most wire texts use Bonnet/Bonnett, and 'John Bennett' appears only in the Dallas Herald.
The fuller dispatch says Wednesday night; the Sept. 15 dates appear to come from the wire's dateline being read as the date of the lynching.
